Oct 27 : Robinhood Markets reported a drop in third-quarter profit on Tuesday as slower cryptocurrency trading weighed on growth, despite robust trading activity across other asset classes, sending its shares down 3.4 per cent after the bell. Crypto markets have come under pressure this year amid heightened volatility and persistent outflows, as inflationary pressures and higher interest rates make bonds and other traditional investments more attractive than speculative assets. Meanwhile, tensions in the Middle East tensions rattled global markets during the quarter, spurring trading activity on brokerage platforms as investors adjusted portfolios and hedged against risks. Robinhood's transaction-based revenue rose about 19 per cent to $867 million, driven by strength in equities, options and prediction markets. The Menlo Park, California-based company posted a profit of $476 million, or 51 cents per share, for the three months ended September 30, compared with $556 million, or 61 cents per share, in the year-ago period.

Source: Reuters

Oct 27 : Visa reported a jump in fourth-quarter profit on Tuesday as customers swiped their cards to pay for travel, shopping and dining out. US consumer spending has remained resilient in the face of persistent inflationary pressures, underpinned by a strong labor market and wage growth. The FIFA World Cup, which ran from June 11 to July 19, also helped boost activity across Visa's network as it brought many visitors to the United States. Payments volume, a gauge of consumer and business spending on Visa's network, jumped 9 per cent in the quarter. The world's largest payment processor's net income was $6 billion, or $3.19 per share, in the three months ended September 30, compared with $5.1 billion, or $2.62 per share, a year earlier.

ZURICH, Oct 27 : Logitech International on Tuesday reported a better-than-expected profit for the second quarter, with the computer mouse and keyboard maker seeing higher demand for its gaming and video conferencing devices. The Swiss-U.S. company reported non-GAAP operating income of $231 million for the three months to the end of September, beating forecasts for $204 million in a consensus gathered by Visible Alpha and the company's own guidance for $185 million to $210 million. Sales rose 3 per cent to $1.22 billion, in line with analyst forecasts and towards the upper end of the company's own outlook of $1.19 billion to $1.22 billion. Logitech said the growth was driven by strong performance in the United States, as well as video collaboration and gaming products, while profit margins also rose as the company achieved a more favourable product mix and faced lower import tariffs into the US.

LOS ANGELES, Oct 27 : UPS CEO Carol Tome told Reuters on Tuesday the AI data center boom is a decades-long opportunity for the world's largest parcel delivery and logistics company, which aims to boost profits by handling fewer, but more premium, shipments.   Global data center spending is estimated to hit roughly $1 trillion in 2026 and more than double before the end of the decade as tech giants like Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon invest billions of dollars in artificial intelligence facilities, which require significant new electricity infrastructure to power and cool servers and computer chips.  The logistics opportunity associated with data centers is $15 billion per year, said Tome.  "It is from manufacturing floor to front door," she said. UPS is flying in critical components such as advanced microprocessors, arranging ocean shipments for equipment of all shapes and sizes, warehousing goods and delivering parts to project sites.

Tome spoke after UPS raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts on better-than-expected third-quarter earnings. Data center projects have become divisive as communities weigh job creation and economic growth against electricity prices, water use and noise. Investors separately are questioning companies' massive investments in them. Nevertheless, there are many projects underway and once those are built, there will continue to be demand for parts and equipment to keep them running, Tome said. "This is something that's going to be decades," Tome said of demand. While UPS data center revenue is growing quickly, it has not yet matched revenue from its healthcare segment, which hit $3 billion in the latest quarter, Tome said, declining to give a figure for the newer business. INFLECTION POINT As part of Tome's "better, not bigger" growth strategy, UPS has been reconfiguring its network to be smaller, nimbler and more profitable.  It has consolidated facilities to reduce costs and improved service quality by investing in things like temperature sensors as well as package scanning and tracking. It also has focused on high-growth and high-margin segments like healthcare, returns and, most recently, data centers.   UPS has made significant headway in specialized healthcare logistics, shipping temperature-controlled chemotherapy drugs, cancer treatments and direct-to-consumer GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. It is now the largest player in the $148 billion global healthcare market after some key acquisitions and internal growth.    That business generated revenue of $6 billion for UPS in 2020 and is forecast to reach $13 billion in revenue this year, Tome said.   UPS is racing rival FedEx for the same high-margin volume as they each wean off low-margin to unprofitable deliveries of online purchases and other goods. FedEx, which has set up a dedicated team to court data center-related business, will report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday. Meanwhile, retailers like Amazon.com  and Walmart as well as growing rivals like OnTrac are aggressively targeting domestic shipments in certain parts of the country. Some of that includes volume UPS and FedEx don't want.  UPS has cut doorstep deliveries of millions of packages for Amazon that it considered unprofitable, which helped lift its margin. Tome said the margin would keep improving every year. "We've moved through an important inflection point," Tome said.

NEW YORK, Oct 27 : The US Federal Election Commission's website has been targeted by a hacker or hackers, disrupting the agency's electronic filings system a week before the November 3 elections, according to an email seen by Reuters. In a statement, the FEC said that, "at this time, the FEC’s electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service." The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said that users could still search the website for past reports. It declined further comment on the outage. The hacking attempts come a week before the midterm elections, which will determine whether President Donald Trump's Republicans maintain their majorities in Congress for the next two years.  The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters' ability to cast ballots.

Oct 27 : The Federal Communications Commission said Tuesday it has approved Amazon Leo’s $11.5 billion deal to acquire Globalstar as the retail giant's satellite arm aims to build a satellite-based communications network to take on Elon Musk's SpaceX Starlink unit. Amazon Leo has launched more than 300 satellites since April 2025 and aims to deploy about 3,200 satellites in Earth's low orbit by 2029. Through the deal, Amazon adds Globalstar's two dozen satellites to its existing network of more than 200 and its mobile-satellite spectrum. Amazon, which has committed to investing more than $10 billion in Leo, is preparing to roll out its commercial satellite services by the end of 2026, the FCC said. The FCC said the companies’ assets will boost Amazon Leo’s entry into the direct-to-device market and allow the satellite-operator to offer fixed and mobile services. "The FCC has empowered Amazon Leo to deliver fast, next-gen satellite broadband services, increase competition, and help communities stay connected all across the country," FCC Chair Brendan Carr said.

NEW YORK, Oct 27 : A US regulator is investigating whether prediction market operator Polymarket violated a 2022 enforcement deal in which it promised to ban US users from its main overseas platform, reviving an inquiry the agency shuttered last year without bringing charges, said two people familiar with the matter. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is probing whether Polymarket took sufficient steps to keep US users off the platform as part of a broader investigation it opened into the company earlier this year, the people said. One of the people said the scrutiny is focused on Polymarket's past controls and processes. The agency is examining Polymarket's controls for determining where customers are located, as well as its advertising activities in the United States, as part of that inquiry, the people said. Polymarket is based in New York and has an offshore entity registered in Panama.

The CFTC is also scrutinizing Polymarket's US platform, which the company began rolling out late last year, including its customer onboarding processes and customer protections, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential enforcement issues. Reuters is reporting these elements of the probe for the first time. The Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg News and other media first reported in June that the CFTC was broadly probing Polymarket, but provided few details. Bloomberg added that the CFTC was looking into social media activity tied to the company. Spokespeople for the CFTC and Polymarket declined to comment. Probes are not necessarily an indication of wrongdoing and many do not result in enforcement action.  The new details, nevertheless, raise fresh questions over why the CFTC and Justice Department last year closed similar probes into whether Polymarket had violated the 2022 settlement, which resolved CFTC allegations at the time that Polymarket had been operating in the US unlawfully since its launch in 2020.  Neither agency has commented on the decision to close the probes and a Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment for this story. Prediction markets allow traders to bet on real-world events, including sports, government policy announcements and elections. Aided by supportive policies under President Donald Trump's second administration, the industry has surged over the past two years. Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr, is a Polymarket investor.  As the platforms have grown, they have drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers and advocacy groups worried the platforms are creating new avenues for insider trading, while recent political upsets, including in Brazil this week, have raised questions about their accuracy. Polymarket has said it has revamped controls. The firm says it expressly prohibits the use of virtual private networks (VPNs) or similar tools to circumvent its geographic restrictions, and has extensive controls to monitor for misconduct and to prevent restricted users from accessing its offshore platform.  Speaking to Reuters in August, Shana Bautista, Polymarket's global head of investigations and intelligence, said US users circumventing its restrictions was not "a really prevalent issue."  BIDEN ADMINISTRATION AGENCIES OPENED PROBE IN 2024 Under the 2022 settlement negotiated by the CFTC's former Biden-era leadership, Polymarket agreed to stop offering its market to US users. But as 2024 US election bets on the platform grew, political pundits and social media users questioned whether Americans were circumventing Polymarket's restrictions.   Months before the election, the CFTC opened a probe into whether Polymarket was complying with the deal, Reuters and other media reported at the time. The Justice Department opened a related investigation, with the FBI searching Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan's New York home in November 2024. Two months later, the Trump administration took office and appointed new leaders to both agencies. On July 15, 2025, Coplan said in an X post that the CFTC and Justice Department had closed their probes and cleared the company of any wrongdoing. A week later, Polymarket said it had bought a CFTC-licensed derivatives exchange, which became the platform for its US operation. CFTC-registered platforms must comply with certain customer protection and market abuse prevention requirements. While CFTC data shows the agency's overall enforcement activity has slumped during Trump's second presidency, its enforcement director David Miller said during his first month on the job in March that he would aggressively police prediction markets.  In April, the agency and Justice Department charged a US soldier, alleging he made $400,000 from insider bets on Polymarket's offshore platform, sparking fresh questions about its controls.  According to the indictment, Gannon Ken Van Dyke, who has pleaded not guilty, accessed the platform using a VPN and "exit mode," which geolocated to a foreign country. Polymarket said at the time that it had referred the matter to the authorities.

BENGALURU, Oct 27 : High inflation will persist in the global economy well into next year, according to hundreds of economists polled by Reuters, who are now increasingly concerned that price pressures will become entrenched beyond rising energy costs caused by the conflict in the Middle East. More than $1 trillion of investment in artificial intelligence technology globally since last year has made some economies more resilient at a time when cost of living pressures are squeezing households and shaping national politics. Most central banks have raised interest rates only a few times or not at all, but more could come if inflation pressures broaden. A global rout in bond markets in recent months has also tightened financial conditions through higher yields. Crude oil prices, which have stayed above $100 a barrel since October 7, hit a six-month high of over $117 last week and are up more than 60 per cent since the US-Israeli war with Iran began almost eight months ago.

Even forecasters who did not anticipate a quick end to the war are now sounding more concerned about inflation resurgence, particularly given the resilience of global growth. More than 500 economists Reuters surveyed globally this month raised their 2027 inflation forecasts for 31 of the 50 economies polled on and growth forecasts for 23 of them. "I am getting much more concerned about inflation again," said Janet Henry, global chief economist at HSBC. "The longer the situation evolves and escalates in the Middle East and the higher the broad basket of price pressures builds, the greater the likelihood that we get not just higher but more persistent inflation." Economists raised 2027 inflation forecasts for 15 of 21 developed economies covered. That suggests inflation worries are spreading and affecting economies that typically experience low price pressures. Cumulatively, median forecasts for 2027 inflation over the past three quarterly polls have risen by 0.7 per centage points for Britain, 0.5 per centage points for the euro zone and only 0.2 per centage points so far for the US. They have risen by 0.4 per centage points for India and by 0.5 per centage point for Brazil. "Higher energy prices continue to ripple through the global economy, but economic activity remains resilient, supported by the AI-led investment cycle and firmer-than-expected activity across several regions," Seth Carpenter, global chief economist at Morgan Stanley, said in a note. "The inflation picture has become more complex as signs of energy pass-through into core measures are beginning to emerge." The effects of rising prices on household budgets have taken centre stage in various political campaigns across the world. Opinion polls show voters ahead of US midterm elections on November 3 are preoccupied with these issues and Brazil's presidential election, which gave incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva his fourth non-consecutive term, was also fought on cost of living issues. In contrast to two previous polls in April and July, which painted a weak-growth, high-inflation scenario, the latest forecasts lean towards one where price pressures accompany more robust economic performance. Economists upgraded their global growth forecasts for both this year and next, to 3.0 per cent and 3.2 per cent, respectively, from 2.9 per cent and 3.1 per cent in the July poll, though the 2027 forecast is lower than the 3.4 per cent the International Monetary Fund is predicting. The US, which leads in AI capital expenditure that has now become the main driver of domestic growth, is forecast to expand 2.3 per cent this year and 2.1 per cent in 2027. While many aerospace companies are struggling to increase output, Boeing is recovering from years of crises and controversies that dented its reputation, drained cash and saddled it with a heavy debt load. That may make investors more inclined to sell shares, even though Boeing's long-term outlook remains good due to high demand for jetliners and only one major competitor, Europe's Airbus, said Tony Bancroft, an investment analyst with Gabelli Funds investment group. The market is going to punish any delay in increasing cash flow, he said. Boeing expects to generate $3 billion next year, lower than Wall Street's consensus projection of $5.5 billion due to lower deliveries and higher capital investment, Jefferies analyst Sheila Kahyaoglu said in a research note on Tuesday. The company posted free cash flow of $464 million in the most recent quarter; for the year so far it has burned through $359 million in cash, but it still expects to generate $2 billion by the end of the year. Boeing reported an adjusted loss of 34 cents per share for the quarter through September, compared with an expected loss of 21 cents, according to data compiled by LSEG. Shares were down 9.6 per cent to $170.23 in afternoon trading, which would be the stock's worst day since April 3, 2025. PRODUCTION STRUGGLES Boeing now expects to reach its 737 production rate target of 47 jets a month in early 2027. As recently as May, Boeing executives said they would hit that pace this summer. As a result, Boeing will not reach its 500-jet delivery target this year, the company's financial chief Jay Malave said during a conference call with analysts on Tuesday. Wing production continues to be a major constraint, but Boeing still plans to increase to 52 jets a month in the second half of 2027, Ortberg said on the call. To reach that rate, Boeing needs to be producing five jets a month at its new 737 production line in Everett, Washington, which opened in July, and increase fuselage production at the former Spirit AeroSystems plant in Wichita, Kansas. Boeing bought Spirit last year in part due to significant ongoing manufacturing defects. Currently, Boeing is making fuselages at a lower rate while it uses up its existing inventory. Starting now, it has to increase output at Wichita to be in line with 737 output, Ortberg said. Deliveries of the popular single-aisle jetliner are a major driver of Boeing's cash flow, and before Ortberg joined Boeing in 2024, the company had struggled for years with production problems due to rushing rate increases at the expense of quality. Despite pressure to increase 737 output faster, "we're going to be smart about this, stay disciplined, and the outlook is there," Ortberg said. The company continues to struggle with production challenges in its 787 program and a supplier dispute has stalled wing production for 777 freighters and 767s, which includes the KC-46 aerial refueling tanker, as first reported by Reuters on Friday. Shipments for wing production have resumed, but the disruption will show up "over the next few quarters," Malave said. Boeing expects the 777-9 jetliner will be on track for regulator certification by mid-2027, with 10 to 15 deliveries next year. LARGER-THAN-EXPECTED QUARTERLY LOSS The dimmer outlook and a larger-than-expected quarterly loss overshadowed major wins by Boeing in recent months: certification by US regulators of the 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10 and winning the US Navy's sixth-generation F/A-XX fighter contract. "Expectations are rising, and they should. We have a stronger foundation than a year ago, but we also have more work to do to deliver on our backlog, strengthen our culture, and improve how we work every day," Ortberg said in a memo to employees after the results. Revenue at Boeing's commercial airplanes division dipped slightly to $10.7 billion, while the operating loss stood at $697 million for an operating margin of negative 6.5 per cent, compared with negative 48.3 per cent a year ago. The company attributed the performance to less profitable jetliner deliveries and higher production costs, including from its supply chain. At Boeing's defense division, higher deliveries, improved operational performance and a $252-million sale of subsidiary HRL Laboratories contributed to nearly $500 million in quarterly earnings with an operating margin of 6.2 per cent, up from 1.7 per cent a year ago. Boeing Global Services earned $1 billion and posted an operating margin of 18.3 per cent. The US planemaker ended the quarter with $25.2 billion in net debt, down slightly from $25.9 billion at the close of the previous quarter and $30.4 billion a year ago.

LONDON, Oct 27 : AI-generated fashion models present a tantalizing opportunity for brands: the ability to create lifelike images for their retail websites while cutting costs by 90 per cent or more compared to photo shoots with human models. For the modeling industry, the technology poses an existential threat because of scant regulation governing the ownership or use of digital twins. Fashion models face the risk of unpaid replication of their image – or replacement by entirely synthetic models. To understand how AI is upending the economics of fashion modeling, Reuters interviewed 15 model-agency directors and reviewed more than a dozen confidential photo-shoot contracts in which brands including Diesel, Calvin Klein and L'Oreal detailed proposed terms for AI-created alterations and future use of the images. The companies’ contract requests included the right to swap a model's face with another using AI; the creation of a digital clone with no additional compensation to the model; and the right to use images of a model's body to train AI. The terms in the unsigned contracts also included broad legal language that could effectively give a brand leeway to use AI however it wanted.

While some companies are looking to repurpose or modify images of existing models, others are using fully AI-generated models, not based on existing humans. As AI use expands, modeling agencies are seeing bookings decline, photo studios are closing and models are facing the loss of a chunk of their livelihoods: photo shoots by fast-fashion retailers constantly adding new collections to their websites. "Within a year, even the next six months, there's going to be less jobs for models, especially our bread and butter, which is ecommerce," said Adot Gak, a model based in London who has been on the cover of Harper's Bazaar and appeared in campaigns by brands including Balmain and H&M. "If we don't speak up about this, in the next two years the whole industry will just be bots." While some fast-fashion players like Spain’s Mango have already rolled out AI-generated models at scale, high-end brands are moving more cautiously. Moncler experimented early with an AI-generated campaign in 2023, and Gucci caused controversy in fashion circles when it posted images generated by AI on Instagram this year.  Moncler said it does not currently use AI-generated models, either on its website or in its campaigns. Gucci did not respond to requests for comment.  "The scariest part is that now people cannot differentiate between a real model and an AI model," said Gak. FACE SWAPS AND 'DIGITAL TWINS' AI allows retailers to endlessly rework and redeploy a model’s image wearing different outfits at a fraction of the cost of new shoots.  "Some brands ask to modify faces, bodies, skin, age or expressions after shoots using AI. Others are asking about creating 'digital twins' of models that they can reuse later without needing another production," said Patrick Staal, owner of modeling agency Uniko Models in Barcelona. In a photo-shoot casting sheet, Italian brand Diesel asked models to agree to "alteration or reconstruction of facial features and body proportions,” along with “swapping of faces among the participating models,” and “superimposition of the Participant’s face onto another person’s body.” Diesel's parent company OTB told Reuters the model release was drafted for a specific campaign and isn’t representative of its typical agreements. It said it doesn’t systematically modify models with AI. Reale Actives – the skincare brand launched this year by social-media personality Alix Earle – uses the tagline, "Reale you is perfect you." But in a contract seen by Reuters, the brand asked for rights to create AI-generated replicas of models and to "own" and use these fakes for a year without further compensation. Reale Actives said in a statement that it uses real models and hasn’t replicated any model using AI. It said the contract language came from a partner production company, which it declined to name. MODELS TRAINING THEIR MACHINE REPLACEMENTS?  In some cases, models are helping to train their replacements: some contracts’ fine print includes language allowing the use of their images to train AI tools.  A Calvin Klein draft contract seen by Reuters asked the model to accept, for no extra pay, that the brand “may use reasonably unrecognizable images of Model (no identifying features such as Model's face, scars, tattoos or otherwise) to train and fine tune AI tools for learning general model attributes.” A Calvin Klein spokesperson said in a statement: "Like many others, we are testing and learning in this fast-moving space," adding that the brand's AI use is guided by regulation, industry standards and respect for models' rights. In many cases, contracts include wording such as "including" or "not limited to," which lawyers commonly use to claim rights that aren’t spelled out. Melanie Howard, partner and chair of luxury brands at law firm Loeb & Loeb in Los Angeles, represents both brands and talent in contract negotiations and said such sweeping language "is dangerous in its ambiguity” and makes it difficult for models to challenge any unsanctioned use of their images. In a photo-shoot contract seen by Reuters, France’s L'Oreal asked for "the right to use artificial intelligence (AI) technologies... including for the purpose of modifying, enhancing, or adapting the appearance of cosmetic products, packaging, or shades, as well as for retouching purposes." Without addressing that contract language, L'Oreal said it uses standard AI tools in post-production and editing that don't affect the model's image. 'WE ARE SAVING SO MUCH MONEY' Some firms are openly embracing AI to replace models and save money.  Europe's biggest online-fashion retailer, Zalando, has rapidly adopted AI-generated imagery for marketing content – and shut both its photo studios in Berlin last year. Fast-fashion retailer About You, which Zalando acquired in July last year, also closed its studio. Overall, Zalando cut more than 340 jobs, though the company said it retained some of those employees in other roles. Now, About You is launching its Scayle Studios business, which creates digital imagery for other retailers using AI-generated models and promises a more than 90 per cent production-cost reduction. Scayle has 130 brand clients and has generated 190,000 outfits in the last month, according to a company spokesperson. "We are saving so much money," said Julian Jansen, vice president of marketing at About You. "You've always had this super fast world of ecommerce, and this super slow traditional world of photo shoots, it didn't fit together in any way – and now with AI, it's a completely different scale." LITTLE REGULATION Regulations globally haven’t kept pace with the threat to models’ livelihoods, but the New York State Fashion Workers Act is one exception. The law has made it illegal since June 2025 for brands to create or modify replicas of models without their explicit consent.  "The misuse of models' images is not new, but with AI that problem is accelerated tenfold," said Sara Ziff, founder and executive director of the New York-based nonprofit Model Alliance, which backed the legislation. Ziff, herself a model for years, pushes for similar laws in other states and federally.  The British Fashion Model Agents Association has drawn up an AI code of practice, including that AI can only be used with the consent of a model, who would own any digital twin. But BFMA head John Horner said that without binding regulation in Britain or Europe, models still risk being taken advantage of by less scrupulous agents. "A lot of young talents don’t fully understand the long-term consequences yet," said Staal, the Barcelona-based model agency director. "Signing away AI rights at 20 years old could still affect someone ten years later."

Source: Reuters

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 27 : Few public companies claim to have the future of humanity on the line while making mundane choices about board composition. Not so with Anthropic. Having warned that its artificial intelligence could one day cure cancer or kill up to 8 billion people, Anthropic has set up a complex plan for who can govern the company as its technology rapidly progresses, its Monday IPO filing showed. Its expected $1.5 trillion valuation would make Anthropic the world's most highly valued public benefit corporation, a setup under Delaware law that means the AI lab must balance investor interests with promoting a wider good. More than fine print, Anthropic's setup may have big implications for investors and a public increasingly adopting the San Francisco-based company's AI. The details show how Anthropic has insulated itself from investor pressure so it can pursue what it says is best for humanity.

Anthropic gave 50.1 per cent voting power over certain matters to its seven co-founders, who, according to the filing, are "distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission," Reuters previously reported. Though an independent trust will control a majority of board seats, the co-founders' supervoting power will extend to elections of the remaining directors and shareholder proposals generally. The Monday filing revealed still more intricacies to overseeing a business that Anthropic expects will outlive the tight-knit crew that created it. Once most of its co-founders are out of the picture and their "Class F" supervoting stock is gone, Anthropic's board will divide into three similarly sized groups, serving three-year terms. Staggering directors' reelection like in the US Senate, Anthropic has embraced a structure once popular as a way to stem hostile takeovers. The company has long voiced concern about the risks of AI falling into authoritarian or nefarious hands. That structure also goes against some corporate-governance tides. In this century, major US companies have largely moved to electing all directors annually, making companies more responsive to shareholder demands on areas like executive pay or strategy. Anthropic declined to comment. 'LONG-TERM FLEXIBILITY' Beyond its board, Anthropic has another governing body with its own set of rules: its long-term benefit trust. Currently chaired by global health leader Neil "Buddy" Shah, the trust controls a special share class called "Class T" stock that will let it elect a majority of Anthropic's board. Anthropic has contemplated what happens if that stock goes away, too. The goal of such eventualities is to "preserve long-term flexibility if circumstances change," its filing said. Even if someone not bound by Anthropic's mission to benefit humanity takes hold of its Class T stock, Anthropic's setup would require directors to follow "provisions relating to our public benefit purpose." Ultimately, the trust's power over the board makes Anthropic a "controlled company" under Nasdaq rules, exempting it from following some typical requirements like having an independent nominating and corporate governance committee. Anthropic is using that exemption to put Daniela Amodei, its president and sister of CEO Dario Amodei, on that committee. THE LEADERS IN CHARGE Anthropic set up a safety and risk committee on its board as well, currently made up of Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan and former Trump White House official Chris Liddell. Billionaire Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings is Anthropic's current lead independent director. Still, Anthropic's seven co-founders — the Amodei siblings among them — remain at the core of governance for the foreseeable future. This partly is through the existence of an entity called "Founder LLC," which, after the trust, will have the biggest say in board elections.

Source: Reuters

A US federal judge on Monday (Oct 27) granted Alibaba Group Holding's request for a preliminary injunction, ordering the US government not to deny Pentagon contracts to companies because they, their parent companies or subsidiaries do business with firms that engage in lobbying activities for the e-commerce giant. Alibaba sued the US government in June after the Pentagon added it to a list of companies allegedly aiding China's military , alongside internet search provider Baidu, EV maker BYD and other major Chinese manufacturing and technology firms. Monday's ruling means Alibaba will be able to retain US lobbyists who also represent Pentagon contractors, removing a potential obstacle to the company's efforts to challenge its designation as a Chinese military company. Alibaba fired dozens of its Washington lobbyists after the Pentagon action in June, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter who was not authorised to speak to the media.

The designation does not impose formal sanctions, but restricts Pentagon contracts with listed companies and, from 2027, purchases of their products or services through third parties. Other listed Chinese tech firms were also concerned about the designation's impact on international lobbying activities as well as the indirect procurement ban, which would completely remove Chinese products from US defence contractors' supply chains, the source added. Alibaba has denied any military ties, saying its products and services are built for retail, logistics, and enterprise technology rather than defence or intelligence. "The determinations have no basis in fact or law," Alibaba said in its lawsuit in June, seeking its removal from the list.

Monday's injunction does not remove Alibaba from the Pentagon list, which the company is continuing to challenge in court. Alibaba did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the injunction. COMPANIES TAKE LEGAL ACTION Alibaba is one of several Chinese firms taking legal action to challenge their placement on the Pentagon's list. Last month, two subsidiaries of the world's largest electric vehicle maker BYD sued the US Department of Defence over a federal law banning any Pentagon contractors from hiring lobbyists that also work with blacklisted firms, arguing that it breached BYD's First Amendment rights. In August, DJI, the world's largest drone maker, appealed its inclusion on the blacklist with the court finding merit in its argument that unclassified records did not support the conclusion that the company contributed to the Chinese defence industrial base. The appeals court ordered the lower court to reconsider its decision to reject DJI's bid to be removed from the Pentagon list and the case is ongoing. The same month, biotech firm WuXi AppTec Co also won a preliminary injunction from a US federal court, which blocked its inclusion on the list. WuXi said the Pentagon designation was politically motivated.
